 The Average Social Security Check Is Just $1,940 And 56% Can’t Afford To Miss Half A Payment — ‘This Is Why Seniors Are Bagging Groceries at 70’

 Retirement sounds wonderful until someone has to explain how the bills get paid. For some Americans, 65 means freedom, travel and finally ditching the alarm clock. For others, it means figuring out how to make Social Security cover a mortgage, groceries and everything else that refuses to get cheaper. 
 That gap was at the center of a post on Reddit's r/AskAnything , where one user asked, "Why do younger generations think boomers can magically retire at the age of 65?" 
 The poster argued that the assumption overlooks a basic financial reality. Americans can claim Social Security retirement benefits as early as 62, but doing so means accepting a reduced monthly payment. For people born in 1960 or later, the full retirement age is 67.

 The post cited an average monthly Social Security benefit of $1,940 and pointed to a Nationwide Retirement Institute survey that found 56% of American adults couldn't financially manage missing even half of a monthly Social Security payment. 
 The Social Security Administration recently announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, which will raise the average retirement benefit by roughly $75 a month starting in January. Even with that increase, many retirees say the adjustment still struggles to keep up with rising costs. 
 The poster connected those numbers to a familiar sight in grocery stores, where older workers can be found bagging groceries, stocking shelves and helping customers. The explanation, according to the post, isn't that every senior wants to keep working. It's that many can't afford not to. 
 'This Is Why Seniors Are Bagging Groceries At 70' 
 One commenter summed up that point in a short, pointed response. 
 "This is why seniors are bagging groceries at 70."

 Others offered different perspectives on what retirement looks like in practice. 
 "A lot can retire early. Most can't. The ones retiring early are not relying on Social Security," one commenter wrote. 
 Another commenter, a Gen Xer planning to retire at 62 , said the goal wasn't necessarily to stop working altogether. Instead, the person hoped to leave a stressful, full-time job and potentially take seasonal work in a tourist town or work as a golf caddie. 
 Story Continues Not everyone agreed that an older person working in a grocery store must be struggling financially. One commenter argued that some people over 65 keep working for extra cash, to stay busy or simply because they enjoy having a job. 
 That commenter also cited estimates suggesting that roughly 18% to 20% of Americans 65 and older work, with the share closer to 30% among those ages 65 to 74. 
 Another commenter pushed back against blaming baby boomers for today's economic pressures, arguing that many had expected a retirement similar to that of earlier generations but faced a different financial reality. 
 The comments pointed to a distinction between people who work because they want to and those who work because they need the paycheck. A grocery store job doesn't reveal which situation applies.

 The $1,940 Question Goes Beyond Social Security 
 The average monthly benefit doesn't tell the whole story. Social Security payments vary based on earnings history, claiming age and benefit type, meaning some retirees receive substantially more or less than the average. 
 For someone with savings, a paid-off home and another source of income, Social Security can provide a useful foundation. For someone paying rent, covering medical bills and managing rising grocery costs, the same payment can be stretched thin. 
 Claiming benefits early can make the math harder. Workers who claim at 62 generally receive less each month than those who wait until full retirement age. But waiting isn't always realistic for people who lose their jobs, face health problems or simply can't afford to keep working. 
 That leaves a question bigger than whether older Americans should retire at 65. Can they afford to? 
 For people approaching retirement, a financial advisor can help estimate future income, review savings and compare Social Security claiming strategies. Finance Advisors connects people with vetted financial advisors who can help them explore their options and plan around their financial goals.

 Building Wealth Across More Than Just The Market 
 Building a resilient portfolio means thinking beyond a single asset or market trend. Economic cycles shift, sectors rise and fall, and no one investment performs well in every environment. That's why many investors look to diversify with platforms that provide access to real estate, fixed-income opportunities, precious metals, and even self-directed retirement accounts. By spreading exposure across multiple asset classes, it becomes easier to manage risk, capture steady returns, and create long-term wealth that isn't tied to the fortunes of just one company or industry. 
 EquityMultiple 
 For accredited investors looking beyond stocks and bonds, EquityMultiple provides access to vetted commercial real estate deals starting at $5,000 , with only ~5% of opportunities passing their due diligence process. 
 Arrived 
 Backed by Jeff Bezos, Arrived Homes makes real estate investing accessible with a low barrier to entry. Investors can buy fractional shares of single-family rentals and vacation homes starting with as little as $100 . This allows everyday investors to diversify into real estate, collect rental income, and build long-term wealth without needing to manage properties directly. 
 American PowerGen 
 As artificial intelligence drives a surge in electricity demand, reliable power generation is becoming a critical part of the technology ecosystem. American PowerGen is developing natural gas-fired power plants in Texas, a fast-growing market fueled by AI data centers, manufacturing expansion, and population growth. By advancing projects through permitting, fuel supply, and grid interconnection, the company is positioning itself to help meet rising energy needs while offering investors exposure to the infrastructure supporting the next wave of AI and industrial growth. 
 Bito 
 As AI coding tools take on more of the work traditionally done by developers, companies are facing new challenges around code quality, context and the rising cost of AI-powered development. Bito is building software designed to help AI coding agents better understand complex codebases while helping companies control AI development costs. Founded by former PubMatic executives, Bito has raised more than $10 million from institutional and individual investors and is now raising additional capital through a Wefunder offering, giving investors an opportunity to invest in a company targeting an emerging need within the rapidly expanding AI software market. 
 FarmTogether 
 Farmland has historically held its value through market volatility and delivered returns uncorrelated to stocks and bonds. For accredited investors, FarmTogether offers direct access to high-quality U.S. farmland starting at $15,000 — fully managed, with no landlord headaches. 
 Fundrise 
 Private real estate and private credit can add income and stability to a stock-heavy portfolio. Fundrise offers access to diversified private real estate and credit strategies through an easy-to-use platform, with professionally managed portfolios designed to generate passive income and long-term growth.
